articles.title: A Burst-Timing Test: Does Free Inference Hold Up at Your Busiest Hour?
articles.excerpt: Free model access rarely collapses on average latency. It collapses inside your busiest ninety minutes, when everyone on the shared path wants the same GPU at the same time. So the only comparison wor…
articles.body: Free model access rarely collapses on average latency. It collapses inside your busiest ninety minutes, when everyone on the shared path wants the same GPU at the same time. So the only comparison worth running is a burst test scheduled at the hours you actually work, not a single quiet-afternoon benchmark. Below is a decision guide I use to choose between a free hosted lane, a free server running your own runtime, a paid hosted lane, and hardware you own. The core claim is simple: pick your inference lane by how it behaves in your peak window, then by ops load, and only then by sticker price. Price per thousand tokens is a tiebreaker, not a starting point. If a lane cannot clear your floor at 16:00 on a Tuesday, its cheapness is a rounding error on the cost of a missed deadline. 1.

articles.title: The Prompt Changed, the Schema Didn't, and the Job Still Passed
articles.excerpt: Version skew is the quietest bug class in model pipelines. Validation passes because the schema never moved. Your prompt did. That gap is where I lost a week. Here is the walkthrough, plus the harness…
articles.body: Version skew is the quietest bug class in model pipelines. Validation passes because the schema never moved. Your prompt did. That gap is where I lost a week. Here is the walkthrough, plus the harness I now use to catch it. The symptom: green checks, wrong totals The extraction job ran nightly. It pulled invoice lines and wrote normalized amounts. One morning the totals were low. No exceptions. No retries. No dead letters. The validator was happy. Every record had amount as a string. That was the only rule. So what did the tests actually cover? Type shape. Nothing else. Not format, not provenance, not drift. Root cause: one sentence in the prompt I had edited the prompt the week before. I added a line asking the model to keep amounts human-readable.

articles.title: Which Setup Step Actually Blocks Your First Run?
articles.excerpt: The step that decides whether a new contributor finishes setup is rarely the step your README spends the most words on. I learned this the boring way: I timed every step of a first run, wrote one JSON…
articles.body: The step that decides whether a new contributor finishes setup is rarely the step your README spends the most words on. I learned this the boring way: I timed every step of a first run, wrote one JSON line per step, and only then saw which step was really eating the first fifteen minutes. The fix that mattered was not better prose for that step, it was a two-second version check that failed loudly before the expensive work started. What follows is the harness I use now, plus the two habits that stopped me from guessing when a run failed. Aggregate setup time is a polite fiction When someone tells you setup takes ten minutes, ask them what they actually measured. They usually measured their own last successful run, on a warm cache, on the machine they have been using for a year.

articles.title: 'Star Trek' legend and sci-fi luminary Walter Koenig dies at 90
articles.excerpt: The man who portrayed the U.S.S. Enterprise’s Pavel Chekov has left us after a 60-year stage and screen career
articles.body: The " Star Trek " community lost one of its most beloved icons on Sunday, October 25, with the sad passing of Walter Koenig at the age of 90 in his North Hollywood home. Koenig was best known as the U.S.S. Enterprise's Russian navigator Pavel Andreievich Chekov for two seasons on "Star Trek: The Original Series." The popular American actor continued in that role for Paramount's first seven "Star Trek" films, which began in 1979's " Star Trek: The Motion Picture " and ended with 1994's " Star Trek: Generations ." A native of Chicago, Illinois, Marvin Walter Koenig was born on Sept. 14, 1936, to Lithuanian immigrant parents and spent his formative years in New York City.

articles.title: What causes mysterious long delayed radio echoes in Earth's atmosphere?
articles.excerpt: Baffling long radio echo delays have prompted a range of potential explanations, most of which focus on a variety of unexplained natural phenomena occurring in Earth's atmosphere.
articles.body: In 1927, Norwegian civil engineer and amateur radio operator Jørgen Hals made an unusual discovery: while monitoring transmissions from a shortwave radio station in Eindhoven, The Netherlands, he began hearing odd, "delayed" radio echoes, arriving approximately three seconds after the original transmissions, that sometimes accompanied the station's signals. "From where this echo comes I cannot say for the present," Hals wrote of his peculiar discovery, adding that he could "only confirm that I really heard it." Almost a century after Hals' discovery, the exact cause of this unusual phenomenon — known today as long delayed echoes, or LDEs — remains unknown.

articles.body: A new stack of Starlink satellites is now in orbit following an early morning SpaceX launch from California. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off at 3:25 a.m. EDT (0725 GMT) on Oct. 27, from from Pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base. The rocket delivered the 27 satellites of Starlink Group 15-16 to low Earth orbit (LEO), and successfully executed its first stage booster landing. The mission's booster, B1082, cut its engines and disengaged from Falcon 9's upper stage approximately 2.5 minutes into flight, and adjusted its trajectory for a touchdown on SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You (OCISLY) droneship in the Pacific Ocean. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches 27 Starlink satellites from California on Oct. 23, 2026.

Astroscale made history with its 2024 up-close in-orbit inspection of a discarded Japanese rocket stage during the pioneering ADRAS-J mission in low Earth orbit (LEO), the region of space below altitudes of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). The firm's ELSA-D mission , which ran from 2021 to 2024, was the first commercial endeavor to demonstrate orbital capture technologies in LEO. articles.title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
articles.excerpt: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic…
articles.body: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.  As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure. Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits.
